subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Backward Products and Groups of Ten

tasks_in_class.description: Fill yellow boxes with 1-digit numbers (multiplicands and multipliers) to get given products; fill remaining white boxes with appropriate products. Second puzzle: identify numbers using row and column products in orange and blue boxes.
Match each problem with the appropriate pictorial representation and write the answer: 2×10=2 Tens=__, 5×10=__Tens=__, 8×10=__Tens=__.
What is 10×10 = __ Tens = __? (extending the ×10 pattern to 10 groups of 10 = 100)

time_bands.activity: Students open the chapter at Mystery Matrix, p.184 ("Fill yellow boxes with 1-digit numbers...."). Working in pairs, they reason backward from each given product to find the missing row and column entries, treating the grid as a constraint puzzle. The teacher circulates, probing with 'How did you know?' rather than confirming answers.

Students turn to Times-10, p.184 ("Match each problem with the appropriate pictorial representation...."). They point to the matching dot-array card for 2×10, 5×10, and 8×10, then write the missing tens and totals. The teacher links the dot rows to the phrase '2 Tens', '5 Tens', reinforcing place-value language.

Students read and complete Times-10, p.185 ("What is 10×10 = __ Tens = __?"). Through a quick count round the class — each child naming one group-of-ten — they build toward 10 groups of 10 and record '10 Tens = 100', connecting the repeated-group model to the hundred.

periods.teacher_notes: The Mystery Matrix requires students to work backward from a product to its factors — a reversal of the usual direction of multiplication that many children find surprising; encourage students to try a factor, check the product, and adjust. When transitioning to the Times-10 work, name the dot-array explicitly: each row is one group of ten, and counting the rows gives the number of tens. A common slip is writing the answer without the tens label — insist on the full form '5 Tens = 50' so the place-value language is set from the start.
materials: Small counters or buttons (optional, for checking grid entries)

periods.activity_title: Splitting Pebbles to Build the Times-15 Table

tasks_in_class.description: Count pebbles in a 5×15 arrangement; complete: 5×15 = 5×10 and 5×5 = __ + __ = __.
Construct a times-15 table (1×15 through 10×15) using the 10×15 pebble arrangement, splitting columns into 10 and 5.
What patterns do you see in the times-15 table?
Compare the times-15 table with the times-5 table. What similarities and differences do you notice? Complete the difference column (15−5=10, 30−10=20, ...).

homework.description: Construct other times-tables for numbers from 11 to 20, as done for 15.

time_bands.activity: Using pebbles (or dots drawn on paper) arranged in a 5×15 grid, students physically separate the last 5 columns from the first 10 and count each part. They complete Constructing Tables, p.185 ("Count pebbles in a 5×15 arrangement; complete: 5×15 = 5×10 and 5×5 = __ + __ = __."), recording the split sentence before writing the total.

Students work row by row through Constructing Tables, p.186 ("Construct a times-15 table (1×15 through 10×15)...."), splitting each new row's arrangement into its 10-column and 5-column parts. Each entry is recorded as '3×15 = 3×10 + 3×5 = 30 + 15 = 45', making the distributive step visible before shortening to just the product.

Students examine their completed table, responding to Constructing Tables Q1, p.186 ("What patterns do you see in the times-15 table?") in pairs, then share aloud. They then place the times-5 table alongside and complete Constructing Tables Q2, p.186 ("Compare the times-15 table with the times-5 table...."), filling the difference column and articulating why each difference is a multiple of 10.

periods.teacher_notes: Having used the pebble-split to find individual products like 5×15, students are now extending the same split systematically to build an entire table — the shift from a single computation to a structure is the core conceptual move here. Watch for children who add 15 repeatedly without splitting; prompt them back to the 10+5 form so the distributive reasoning stays visible. A frequent error is writing the difference column as the times-10 table (10, 20, 30…) without connecting it to the comparison: ask 'why is every difference a multiple of 10?' to surface the explanation.
materials: Pebbles or counters (at least 150 per group)

section_titles: Making tables by splitting into equal groups
periods.activity_title: Patterns Across Tables and the Doubling Strategy

tasks_in_class.description: Compare times-1 with times-11, times-2 with times-12, and so on. Share your observations.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.187
tasks_in_class.description: 6×14 = Double of 6×7. Why? (explain the splitting-and-doubling reasoning from the wheel arrangement)

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.188
tasks_in_class.description: Can we construct the times-14 table by splitting and doubling? Try! What other times-tables can be constructed by splitting into equal groups and doubling? Give examples.

time_bands.activity: Students open to Constructing Tables Q4, p.186 ("Compare times-1 with times-11, times-2 with times-12, and so on...."). In small groups they place the two tables side by side and note aloud what is the same and what changes. The teacher records shared observations on the board, pressing for the reason behind each pattern rather than just its description.

Students study the wheel arrangement in Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.187 ("6×14 = Double of 6×7. Why?"). They circle the two identical halves of the wheel, count each, and write '6×7 + 6×7 = 2×(6×7) = 6×14'. The teacher then asks: 'Would this work for 6×16? Why or why not?' — directing attention to the condition of an even multiplier.

Students work through Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.188 ("Can we construct the times-14 table by splitting and doubling? Try!...."). They build at least four entries of the times-14 table using the doubling shortcut and then list two other tables (e.g. times-12, times-18) that the same strategy fits, writing a brief justification beside each.

periods.teacher_notes: The comparison of times-N with times-(N+10) tables in Constructing Tables Q4 extends the splitting insight already established for times-15; naming that content explicitly — 'just as we split 15 into 10 and 5, every table above 10 carries a hidden times-10 piece' — helps students see it as one idea, not two. In the doubling section, the most common confusion is applying the strategy to an odd multiplier (e.g. trying to halve 15 to get 7.5); use the wheel picture to show that the two halves must be equal whole-number groups. Ensure students state which tables are suitable and why, not just list examples.

periods.activity_title: Tens Language: Scaling Up with Place Value

tasks_in_class.description: 10×10=__; 2 times (double of) 10×10=__. Discuss in grade what happens when we take several groups of 10.

time_bands.activity: Students read and complete Multiples of 10, p.188 ("Find the answers: a) 15×10=__Tens=__...."). They write each answer in two forms — the Tens form first, then the numeral — linking back to the flat-and-rod imagery in the book. The teacher emphasises that '15 Tens' is not a guess but a direct reading of the groups.

Class discussion around Multiples of 10, p.188 ("10×10=__; 2 times (double of) 10×10=__."). The teacher draws successive rows of ten-rods on the board as students call out each new total; the class discovers that doubling 10×10 gives 20×10 and articulates the pattern that multiplying the group count by 2 doubles the product.

Students independently tackle Now think and answer, p.189 ("Answer: a) 21×10....") then move straight to Solve the following problems, p.190 ("24×40=__...."), writing their working as a splitting step (e.g. 24×40 = 24×4×10). Two or three children share their methods; the teacher highlights that multiplying by 20 or 40 folds a times-10 step inside.

periods.teacher_notes: The progression here moves from '15 groups of 10' (a single-digit group count scaled by 10) to a 2-digit group count times a multiple of 10, so the Tens-language form is the bridge: students who can write '24 Tens = 240' will handle 24×40 by reading it as 24×4 tens. A very common error is writing 15×10 = 150 correctly but then writing 15×20 = 150 again (forgetting to double); the Tens-language catches this because '15 Tens' and '30 Tens' are visibly different. When students share strategies for Now think and answer, probe each voice: 'Is there a quicker way once you know the ×10 answer?'
materials: Tens-rods (Dienes material) or hand-drawn flat-and-rod sketches

section_titles: A Day at the Transport Museum: 2-digit multiplication and division
periods.activity_title: Area Grids and Grouping: Two-Digit Products and Remainders

tasks_in_class.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
tasks_in_class.description: Find 15×14 using the area-model grid (toy train: 15 coaches × 14 seats). How many children can be seated?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
tasks_in_class.description: Find 324÷14 using the repeated-subtraction table. How many coaches for 324 children? Identify the remainder.
Solve: a) 25×34, b) 16×43, c) 68×12, d) 39×13, e) 125÷15, f) 94÷11, g) 440÷22, h) 508÷18. Also identify remainder (if any) in division problems.

time_bands.activity: Students open to A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191 ("Find 15×14 using the area-model grid...."). They draw the four sub-rectangles (10×10, 10×4, 5×10, 5×4) on squared paper, label each partial product, and add them to reach the total. The transport museum story gives a real count to verify: 'Can 210 children be seated across 15 coaches of 14 seats each?'

Students tackle A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191 ("Find 324÷14 using the repeated-subtraction table...."). They build the repeated-subtraction table step by step — subtracting multiples of 14 from 324 — recording how many groups of 14 have been accounted for at each line and naming the leftover as the remainder.

Students choose four problems from Let Us Solve, p.192 ("Solve: a) 25×34, b) 16×43....") — two multiplication using the area model and two division using the repeated-subtraction table. They circle any remainder found in division problems. Selected students share one solution each, justifying their partial-product or subtraction step aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The area model makes partial products visible as distinct rectangles; stress that the four areas must all be added — a common error is adding only two or three. For division, the repeated-subtraction table can look overwhelming at first; encourage students to begin by subtracting a large multiple of 14 (e.g. 10×14 = 140) to reduce the dividend quickly before taking smaller steps. When students identify a remainder, ask 'Is the remainder smaller than the divisor? How do you know you cannot take out one more group?'

section_titles: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
periods.activity_title: Hundreds Flats: Scaling Multiplication into Hundreds

tasks_in_class.description: 10×100=10 Hundreds=1000. What happens when we put 10 Hundreds together? Complete: 12×100=__, 15×100=__, 27×100=__, 70×100=__.
We Know: 80×100=8000. Find: 80×50=__, 40×50=__. (Use relationship between ×100 and ×50)
11×200 shown three ways. Share what you notice. Then: 11×100=__, 11×200=__, 22×100=__, 22×200=__. What do you notice about any number times-100s?

time_bands.activity: Students read and complete Multiples of 100, p.192 ("Complete: 3×100=__Hundreds=__....") then Multiples of 100, p.192 ("10×100=10 Hundreds=1000...."), writing each result in Hundreds language first. The teacher draws rows of orange 100-flats on the board to make the Hundreds count visible before students write the numeral.

Students work on Now answer (We Know/Find), p.193 ("We Know: 80×100=8000. Find: 80×50=__, 40×50=__."). They discuss in pairs: if ×100 gives 8000, what does ×50 give and why? The teacher presses: 'How is ×50 related to ×100?' to elicit the halving relationship.

Students study three representations of 11×200 in Answer the following questions, p.194 ("11×200 shown three ways....") and write what they notice about each. They then complete the four products and articulate a general statement about multiplying by multiples of 100. The teacher records the shared generalisation on the board in students' own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students arriving at this point have used Tens language for multiplying by 10; the parallel move here is Hundreds language for multiplying by 100, so naming that explicit parallel — 'just as 14 Tens = 140, here 14 Hundreds = 1400' — anchors the extension. The relationship between ×100 and ×50 in Now answer is challenging: many children will halve 8000 to get 4000 but struggle to explain why; insist they articulate the halving-of-the-multiplier reasoning rather than simply producing the answer. The three-way presentation of 11×200 is designed to show method flexibility — ask students which of the three they find clearest and why.
materials: Orange 100-flat Dienes blocks (or hand-drawn squares representing 100 each)

section_titles: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
periods.activity_title: Set A, B, C: Discovering Multiplicative Relationships

time_bands.activity: Students complete Now answer, p.193 ("30×100=__, 40×100=__....") independently, writing each answer swiftly. Answers are shared verbally across the class; the teacher notes any pattern in the last two zeros and invites students to state a quick rule for multiplying by 100.

Students work through Answer the following questions, p.194 ("18×100=__, 15×200=__...."), applying the Hundreds-language and the ×100 shortcut to multiples of 100 such as 200, 300, 500, 800. Two or three students share how they decomposed each multiplier (e.g. '15×200 = 15×2×100 = 30×100 = 3000').

Students tackle Set A/B/C, p.195 ("Find answers in Set A; use relationships to find Set B; answer Set C."). They first complete Set A by computation, then use those anchor values to derive Set B by inspection of relationships, and finally apply the pattern to Set C without fresh computation. Groups share how they moved from Set A to Set B — naming the multiplicative jump — before individual answers are confirmed.

periods.teacher_notes: Now answer and Answer the following questions consolidate the ×100 and ×multiples-of-100 procedures before the more demanding Set A/B/C relationship work; sequence the two practice tasks quickly so the bulk of the unit rests on the Set A/B/C investigation. In Set A/B/C, students must not re-compute Set B from scratch — the point is to derive it from Set A by noticing the multiplicative relationship; circulate and redirect any student who is computing rather than reasoning. Set C items like 44×10 and 22×20 are designed to be answered without fresh computation by connecting them to earlier established facts.

periods.activity_title: Rice Sacks and Related Facts: Division by 10 and 100

tasks_in_class.description: Rice sack problems: a) 60 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks, b) 600 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks. If sack weighs 100 kg, 600÷100=__. Write: 60÷10=__, 600÷10=__, 600÷100=__.
1. Manku sees 870 bananas; each bunch has 10. How many bunches? 2. Rukhma Bi distributes ₹1000 equally among 10 grandchildren. How much each? Write the division statement.

time_bands.activity: Students read the rice-sack story and complete Dividing by 10 and 100, p.197 ("Rice sack problems: a) 60 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks...."). They draw sack groups on paper, count them, and record the three division statements: 60÷10, 600÷10, 600÷100. The teacher highlights that the number of sacks is found by 'how many groups of 10 (or 100) fit inside.'

Students complete Find the answers, p.198 ("40÷10=__, 400÷10=__, 400÷100=__...."), working across the three rows of related facts. In pairs they name the pattern they see moving down each column and across each row, then share with the class. The teacher collects observations and steers toward the generalisation: 'adding a zero to the dividend adds a zero to the quotient when dividing by 10.'

Students solve Think and answer, p.198 ("Manku sees 870 bananas...."), writing a division statement for each story. They then open to Let Us Solve, p.197 ("Also identify remainder (if any): a) 237×28....") and attempt as many problems as the remaining time permits, using the area model for multiplication and repeated-subtraction table for division.

periods.teacher_notes: Division by 10 and 100 parallels the multiplication by 10 and 100 that students have already practised with Tens and Hundreds language; naming that parallel explicitly — 'if 14×10 = 140 Tens, then 140÷10 must give back 14' — helps students see division as an inverse rather than a separate procedure. In Find the answers, the pattern spotting is the learning, not just the answers; prioritise group discussion over quick individual completion. For Let Us Solve, students may not finish all six items — that is expected; the goal is for each student to apply the area model and repeated-subtraction table at least once each.

section_titles: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
periods.activity_title: Multi-Step Stories and the Coins Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Punjab Mail: a) 3 coaches carried 96 passengers — how many per coach? b) Train now has 24 coaches, each carrying 72 passengers — how many can travel?

School trip to Goa (36 children + 6 teachers, double-decker bus): a) seats needed vs. available (15 lower + 10 upper, 2 per seat); b) total ticket cost for all children; c) ticket cost for all teachers.
Kedar's brick kiln: a) 125 bricks/day — how many in a month? b) each brick sold for ₹9 — monthly earnings?
Chilika lake trip (8 people): bus ticket ₹60 each, boat ride ₹1200 for all. How much per person? (multi-step)

Ticket costs ₹750. Bujji uses ₹200 notes, Munna ₹50 notes, Balu ₹20 notes, Chinnu ₹5 coins, Sansu ₹2 coins. a) How many notes/coins each needs; b) who gets no change; c) how long to count Chinnu's coins?

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on Let Us Solve Q1, p.198 ("Punjab Mail: a) 3 coaches carried 96 passengers....") and Let Us Solve Q2, p.199 ("School trip to Goa...."). Each pair writes out every computation step, naming the operation used. Pairs then share answers for Q1 with an adjacent pair, checking division and multiplication steps.

Students tackle Let Us Solve Q3, p.199 ("Kedar's brick kiln: a) 125 bricks/day....") and Let Us Solve Q4, p.199 ("Chilika lake trip (8 people)....") independently. The teacher circulates and prompts students who conflate per-person and total costs to draw a 'total ÷ number of people' frame before computing.

Students open to Chinnu's Coins Q1, p.201 ("Ticket costs ₹750. Bujji uses ₹200 notes...."). They compute how many of each denomination reaches exactly ₹750 (or the nearest multiple) and circle who needs no change. As a closing share, two students explain their reasoning for Chinnu's coin count and the time estimate.

periods.teacher_notes: These word problems require students to choose and chain operations — division to find a per-unit value, then multiplication to scale it — which is the key challenge at this stage; encourage students to name the operation and the unit before computing. In Let Us Solve Q2, the seating calculation has two parts (lower and upper deck, two people per seat) that students often conflate; suggest they find seats on each deck separately and then add. The Chinnu's Coins puzzle introduces denomination-divisibility thinking: ₹750 is not exactly divisible by ₹2, so Sansu must overpay — a productive point of class discussion.

section_titles: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
periods.activity_title: Number Grid Hunt and Closing Pattern Investigation

tasks_in_class.description: Find multiplication and division sentences in the number grid. Shade them. How many can you find? (3 given: 250×4=1000, 50×20=1000, 525÷5=105; find more)

Observe: 12×13=156, 11×14=154, 13×13=169, 11×12=132. In each case, spot a pattern in the two numbers and their product (coloured digits). For what other multiplication problems does this pattern hold? Find 5 such examples.
Match vehicles travelling at full capacity to total passengers: 75 cycles, 52 autos, 103 cars, 20 minibus, 30 aeroplanes, 15 train sleeper coaches.

time_bands.activity: Students open to Let Us Solve Q5, p.200 ("Find multiplication and division sentences in the number grid. Shade them...."). Working individually, they use the three given examples as a model and scan the grid systematically, shading any row, column, or diagonal of numbers that forms a valid multiplication or division sentence. After a set period, pairs compare and verify each other's finds.

Students read Chinnu's Coins Q2, p.201 ("Observe: 12×13=156, 11×14=154...."). They compute each given product, study the coloured digits, and write what they notice. They then generate five examples of their own that fit the same pattern and verify each by multiplication before writing the pattern in words.

Students complete Chinnu's Coins Q3, p.202 ("Match vehicles travelling at full capacity to total passengers...."), multiplying each vehicle count by its capacity and drawing lines to the matching total. The unit closes with two students sharing one pattern they found in the number grid and one pattern from the Chinnu's Coins Q2 investigation.

periods.teacher_notes: The number-grid hunt asks students to apply multiplication and division operationally — they must test candidate triples in the grid rather than compute from a given problem, which reverses the usual direction; remind students that a valid sentence needs three numbers in the grid and a correct operation linking them. Chinnu's Coins Q2 surfaces early algebraic thinking: when one factor increases by 1 and the other decreases by 1 (keeping their sum constant), the product changes in a predictable way — if students generate five examples and all agree, ask 'does this always work and why?' to push toward generalisation. Let Us Solve Q6 is set as an unhurried practice task for outside the classroom given its length.
materials: Coloured pencils or markers (for shading the number grid)

items.section_title: Mystery Matrix
items.prompt: A multiplication grid has rows and columns. The product of one row is 24 and the product of another row is 18. A number appears in both rows. Which of these numbers could appear in both rows?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6, because 6 is a factor of both 24 (4×6) and 18 (3×6).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check which single-digit number divides both 24 and 18 exactly.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 5 suggests the student is guessing rather than checking divisibility; 5 does not divide 24 or 18.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 7 suggests the student may be picking numbers near 6 without testing whether 7 divides 24 or 18.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 8 shows the student recognises 8 divides 24 but has not checked that 8 does not divide 18.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student list factors of 24 and factors of 18 and circle numbers on both lists; stretch: ask them to find a second number that could appear in both rows.

exercise.description: Fill yellow boxes with 1-digit numbers (multiplicands and multipliers) to get given products; fill remaining white boxes with appropriate products. Second puzzle: identify numbers using row and column products in orange and blue boxes.

items.section_title: Times-10: multiplying by 10
items.prompt: Draw 3 rows of 10 dots on your page. Write the multiplication sentence that matches your drawing using Tens language. Then write the total.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 rows of 10 dots drawn; sentence: 3×10 = 3 Tens = 30.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the rows (groups) and write N×10 = N Tens = the numeral.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a printed grid of dots to circle groups; stretch: ask the student to draw 7 rows of 10 and write the matching Tens sentence.

exercise.description: Match each problem with the appropriate pictorial representation and write the answer: 2×10=2 Tens=__, 5×10=__Tens=__, 8×10=__Tens=__.

items.section_title: Constructing Tables by splitting
items.prompt: Show how you would find 4×15 by splitting 15 into 10 and 5. Write each part of your working and then the total.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 15 into 10 and 5, multiply each part by 4, then add the two partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use counters arranged in a 4×15 grid and physically separate the last 5 columns; stretch: ask the student to use the same split to find 7×15 and check by skip-counting.

exercise.description: Construct a times-15 table (1×15 through 10×15) using the 10×15 pebble arrangement, splitting columns into 10 and 5.

items.section_title: Making tables by splitting into equal groups
items.prompt: Riya wants to find 5×18 by splitting and doubling. She says: '5×18 = double of 5×9.' Which table would NOT work with the splitting-and-doubling method?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Times-15, because 15 is odd and cannot be split into two equal whole-number groups.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The doubling strategy requires halving the multiplier to get a whole number, so it works only for even multipliers.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing times-12 shows the student has not checked that 12 is even and can be halved to 6.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing times-16 shows the student has not verified that 16 halves to 8, an even whole number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing times-20 shows the student has not confirmed that 20 halves to 10, so doubling is valid.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try halving each option and see which gives a fraction; stretch: ask the student to name two more odd multipliers to which the strategy cannot apply.

exercise.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.188
exercise.description: Can we construct the times-14 table by splitting and doubling? Try! What other times-tables can be constructed by splitting into equal groups and doubling? Give examples.

items.section_title: Times-10: multiplying by 10
items.prompt: Arjun says: '6×10 = 6 Tens = 60, so 10×10 must be 10 Tens.' Is he right? Write 10×10 in Tens language and give the total. Explain in one sentence why 10 Tens equals the number it does.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, Arjun is right. 10×10 = 10 Tens = 100. Ten groups of ten make one hundred because 10 Tens is the same as one Hundred in the place-value system.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count 10 groups of 10 using Tens language and recognise that 10 Tens bundles into 1 Hundred.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw 10 rows of 10 dots and count the total; stretch: ask the student to write 20×10 in Tens language and explain what happens to 20 Tens.

exercise.description: What is 10×10 = __ Tens = __? (extending the ×10 pattern to 10 groups of 10 = 100)

items.section_title: Constructing Tables by splitting
items.prompt: Look at the times-5 and times-15 tables. The times-5 entry for 3 is 15, and the times-15 entry for 3 is 45. What is the difference? What will the difference be for 7×5 and 7×15? Explain the pattern you see.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The difference for 3 is 45−15=30. For 7: 7×15=105 and 7×5=35, so the difference is 70. The difference is always 10 times the multiplier because 15−5=10, so every times-15 entry exceeds the matching times-5 entry by 10 times that row's multiplier.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the times-5 entry from the times-15 entry for each row and observe that the difference equals the row number times 10.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: pair-share before writing; let the student complete one more row of the difference column first; stretch: ask what the difference column would look like for times-20 versus times-10.

exercise.description: Compare the times-15 table with the times-5 table. What similarities and differences do you notice? Complete the difference column (15−5=10, 30−10=20, ...).

items.section_title: Constructing Tables by splitting
items.prompt: The times-2 table gives: 1×2=2, 2×2=4, 3×2=6. The times-12 table gives: 1×12=12, 2×12=24, 3×12=36. What is the difference between matching entries? Why does this difference stay the same for every row?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The difference for each row is 10 times the row number (10, 20, 30…). This is because 12−2=10, so every times-12 entry is exactly 10 times the row number more than the matching times-2 entry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract each times-2 entry from the matching times-12 entry and notice the result equals 10 × (row number).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write out the first three rows of both tables side by side and subtract; stretch: predict what the difference column for times-3 versus times-13 would look like.

exercise.description: Compare times-1 with times-11, times-2 with times-12, and so on. Share your observations.

items.section_title: Making tables by splitting into equal groups
items.prompt: A class uses the splitting-and-doubling method to find 8×14. They first find 8×7=56. What is 8×14?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Double the result of 8×7 (=56) to get 8×14 = 112.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 98 suggests the student added 56+42 instead of doubling; they may have computed 8×7 + 6×7.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 104 suggests the student added 56+48, possibly confusing 8×7 with 8×6 in one half.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 116 suggests the student added 56 to 60 rather than doubling 56.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw two identical rectangles each showing 8×7 and count all dots; stretch: ask the student to use the same method to find 8×18 and explain whether doubling is still valid.

exercise.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.187
exercise.description: 6×14 = Double of 6×7. Why? (explain the splitting-and-doubling reasoning from the wheel arrangement)

items.section_title: Multiples of 10: multiplying by 10 and 20
items.prompt: 10×10 = 100. What is 2 times (10×10)? Write it in Tens language and as a numeral. Then explain: what happens to the product each time you take one more group of ten groups of ten?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2×(10×10) = 2×100 = 200. In Tens language: 20 Tens = 200. Each time you add one more group of 10 tens, the product increases by 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that each group of 10 tens equals 100, so counting groups of 10-tens counts hundreds.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw rows of ten-rods and count how many hundreds appear after each doubling; stretch: ask the student to predict 5×(10×10) and state it in Hundreds language.

exercise.description: 10×10=__; 2 times (double of) 10×10=__. Discuss in grade what happens when we take several groups of 10.

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: A student writes: '11×100 = 1100 and 11×200 = 2200.' Is the second result double the first? Write a similar pair for 13×100 and 13×200. Explain in one sentence why multiplying by 200 always gives double the result of multiplying by 100.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, 2200 is double 1100. 13×100=1300 and 13×200=2600 (double 1300). Multiplying by 200 gives double because 200=2×100, so the product is also multiplied by 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose ×200 as ×2×100 and apply each factor in turn.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write 200=100+100 and add the ×100 result to itself; stretch: ask the student to predict 13×300 using the same reasoning.

exercise.description: 11×200 shown three ways. Share what you notice. Then: 11×100=__, 11×200=__, 22×100=__, 22×200=__. What do you notice about any number times-100s?

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: You know that 14×100 = 1400 and 14×5 = 70. Use these two facts to find 14×500. Explain each step.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 500 as 5×100, compute 14×5 first, then multiply that result by 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: show the decomposition 500=5×100 written out before the student continues; stretch: ask the student to use Set A/B/C reasoning to find 14×250 from the same anchor facts.

items.section_title: Dividing by 10 and 100
items.prompt: A student fills in this table: 40÷10=4, 400÷10=40, 400÷100=4. She then tries 4000÷100. Which answer fits the pattern?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Dividing by 100 removes two trailing zeros from a multiple of 100.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 4 suggests the student removed three zeros (dividing by 1000 rather than 100).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 400 suggests the student removed only one zero (dividing by 10 rather than 100).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 4000 suggests no division was applied; the student returned the original dividend.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 4000 = 40×100 and ask how many groups of 100 are in 4000; stretch: ask the student to extend the table with 4000÷10 and explain the difference.

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: Look at this number grid entry: 250 × 4 = 1000. A classmate finds 50 × 20 = 1000 in the same grid. Are both correct? Write one more multiplication sentence using only numbers that could appear in such a grid that gives a product of 1000.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, both are correct: 250×4=1000 and 50×20=1000 are valid. One more example: 125×8=1000.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find two numbers whose product is 1000 by splitting 1000 into factor pairs (1000 = 125×8, 200×5, 100×10, etc.).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a list of factors of 1000 and ask them to pair them; stretch: ask the student to find one division sentence using numbers that equal 1000 as the dividend.

exercise.description: Find multiplication and division sentences in the number grid. Shade them. How many can you find? (3 given: 250×4=1000, 50×20=1000, 525÷5=105; find more)

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: Here are two multiplications: 12×13=156 and 11×14=154. One factor went up by 1 and the other went down by 1. Write the product when one factor goes up by 1 again (10×15). What do you notice about the products 156, 154, and your new answer?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 10×15=150. The products are 156, 154, 150 — each decreases (by 2, then by 4). As one factor rises and the other falls by 1 each time (keeping the same sum), the product decreases.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute 10×15 by multiplication, then compare 156, 154, 150 to spot the decreasing pattern.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: compute each product separately before comparing; stretch: ask the student to predict 9×16 and check whether the pattern continues.

exercise.description: Observe: 12×13=156, 11×14=154, 13×13=169, 11×12=132. In each case, spot a pattern in the two numbers and their product (coloured digits). For what other multiplication problems does this pattern hold? Find 5 such examples.

items.section_title: Multiples of 10: multiplying by 10 and 20
items.prompt: What is 17×10 written in Tens language, and what is its value?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write N×10 = N Tens, then convert N Tens to the numeral by placing N in the tens column.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 7 Tens = 70 suggests the student used only the units digit of 17 rather than the full number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 17 Tens = 107 shows the student wrote 1 in the hundreds and 7 in the units, confusing place-value columns.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 10 Tens = 100 shows the student replaced 17 with 10, perhaps misreading the multiplier.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 17 rows of 10 dots and count in tens; stretch: ask the student to write 17×20 in Tens language and compute it.

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: What is 13×100?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write 13×100 = 13 Hundreds and read the place value: 1 Thousand and 3 Hundreds = 1300.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 130 suggests the student multiplied by 10 rather than 100.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 1003 suggests the student appended digits rather than applying place-value reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 13000 suggests the student multiplied by 1000 rather than 100.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw 13 orange 100-flats and count; stretch: ask the student to find 13×200 using this result.

exercise.description: 10×100=10 Hundreds=1000. What happens when we put 10 Hundreds together? Complete: 12×100=__, 15×100=__, 27×100=__, 70×100=__.

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: Find: a) 16×200 b) 9×500. Write each answer as a numeral.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose each multiplier (200 = 2×100; 500 = 5×100), multiply the non-hundred part first, then by 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide the first step written out (16×2=32, then ×100) before the student continues; stretch: ask the student to find 16×400 by doubling their answer to part a).

items.section_title: Multiples of 10: multiplying by 10 and 20
items.prompt: A tempo traveller seats 12 passengers. How many passengers can travel in 10 such tempo travellers? Write your answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply 12 by 10 using Tens language: 12 Tens = 120.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw 10 groups of 12 and count; stretch: ask how many passengers in 20 tempo travellers and whether they can use the ×10 answer to find it.

items.section_title: A Day at the Transport Museum: 2-digit multiplication and division
items.prompt: A museum bus has 12 rows of seats with 13 seats in each row. Use the area model to find the total number of seats. Show all four partial products.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw the area-model grid, label the four sub-rectangles, compute each partial product, and add all four.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a pre-drawn grid with the four sections labelled and ask them to fill in each area; stretch: ask the student to check by using a different splitting (e.g. 12×13 = 12×10 + 12×3).

exercise.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
exercise.description: Find 15×14 using the area-model grid (toy train: 15 coaches × 14 seats). How many children can be seated?

items.section_title: A Day at the Transport Museum: 2-digit multiplication and division
items.prompt: 168 students are to be seated in coaches that each hold 14 students. Use the repeated-subtraction method to find how many coaches are needed and whether any students are left over.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 168÷14=12 coaches exactly; remainder 0. Subtraction: 10×14=140, 168−140=28; 2×14=28, 28−28=0. Total groups = 10+2=12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build the repeated-subtraction table, removing large multiples of 14 first, then count all groups removed and check the remainder.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start the table with 5×14=70 written out and ask the student to continue; stretch: ask what happens if 170 students must board coaches of 14 and identify the remainder.

exercise.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
exercise.description: Find 324÷14 using the repeated-subtraction table. How many coaches for 324 children? Identify the remainder.

items.section_title: Dividing by 10 and 100
items.prompt: A farmer packs 490 oranges into bags of 10. How many bags does he fill? Write the division statement.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 490 by 10 by removing one zero: 490÷10=49.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student group counters in tens and count the groups; stretch: ask the student to find how many bags of 100 could be filled with 4900 oranges.

exercise.description: Rice sack problems: a) 60 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks, b) 600 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks. If sack weighs 100 kg, 600÷100=__. Write: 60÷10=__, 600÷10=__, 600÷100=__.

items.section_title: Dividing by 10 and 100
items.prompt: A shopkeeper earns ₹560 and shares it equally among 10 workers. How much does each worker get? Write the division statement.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 560 by 10 by reading 56 Tens ÷ 10 = 56.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write ₹560 = 56 Tens and ask how many ones are in each equal share; stretch: ask the student to find how much each worker gets if there are 100 workers instead.

exercise.description: 1. Manku sees 870 bananas; each bunch has 10. How many bunches? 2. Rukhma Bi distributes ₹1000 equally among 10 grandchildren. How much each? Write the division statement.

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: A double-decker bus has 10 lower seats and 8 upper seats, with 2 children per seat. How many children can the bus carry in total?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply seats on each deck by 2, then add the two results.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the two decks as separate groups and count; stretch: ask how many buses of this size are needed to carry 108 children.

exercise.description: School trip to Goa (36 children + 6 teachers, double-decker bus): a) seats needed vs. available (15 lower + 10 upper, 2 per seat); b) total ticket cost for all children; c) ticket cost for all teachers.

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: 6 friends go on a boat trip. The boat hire costs ₹900 for all of them together. How much does each friend pay?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total cost by the number of people: 900÷6=150.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use repeated subtraction of 6 from 900; stretch: ask how the answer changes if a seventh friend joins and the total hire remains ₹900.

exercise.description: Chilika lake trip (8 people): bus ticket ₹60 each, boat ride ₹1200 for all. How much per person? (multi-step)

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: A museum ticket costs ₹500. Priya pays using ₹50 notes only. How many ₹50 notes does she need? Write the division statement.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 500 by 50: recognise that 50×10=500, so 10 notes are needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count how many 50s fit into 500 using repeated addition; stretch: ask the student how many ₹20 notes would be needed for the same ticket and whether any notes would be left over.

exercise.description: Ticket costs ₹750. Bujji uses ₹200 notes, Munna ₹50 notes, Balu ₹20 notes, Chinnu ₹5 coins, Sansu ₹2 coins. a) How many notes/coins each needs; b) who gets no change; c) how long to count Chinnu's coins?
